Been a hot minute since I watched it, but the abruptness of the film’s ending seems perfect to me as Judy and Scottie’s obsession with her/fear of heights *is* the movie, so her end would be its end.

Scottie’s vertigo is a manifestation of his death drive — a death drive in overdrive imo, and the only thing that “cures” it is this gross objectification of this woman. Death and sex intertwined, and the perversity of the voyeur (or, to be more specific, the male gaze). What that does to Scottie, to Judy, to the audience, and finally to the film itself. It’s intoxicating in both senses of the word… for me, when I finally “got” the film, I became similarly obsessed with it and watched jt on repeat for awhile. I’d even turn it on to fall asleep to.

But the jig is up when Judy/Madeleine dies. The illusion is shattered and the film appropriately ends on a shock. A sorta *kenjataimu* — post-nut clarity. Disgust, even.

There’s a filmed alternate ending where Jimmy Stewart and Barbara Bel Gedee are sitting at home, listening to a news story on the radio about how the husband has been arrested. It’s maybe a more traditional ending, but I quite like the shock and bleakness of the regular ending.

Wow, this perspective really sheds light on Scotties actions towards Judy. I was also grossed out about Scotts hidden perversity with Judy but I couldn’t make it out on why it fit so well with the overall narrative. Stellar analysis. This also makes the ending all the more fitting.

In all honesty, I also like the regular ending more than this alternate one. I just felt things could’ve been more differently, at the very least, more played out. In my opinion, everything was well paced UNTIL her sudden end. Yet, looking into other people’s perspectives and how the movie portrays Judy’s character, I can see the ending as well fitting. Although for a first time view, it was way too shocking and quick for that satisfying impact, at least for me. However, there WAS an impact, as I am still typing about this film, so I wouldn’t say it was a bad ending!

Vertigo is a movie that I can appreciate but like it less and less on repeat viewings. It’s a bleak ending for sure and a great performance by Stewart, but the ending and the movie itself only work if you buy the central romance of the movie, which I never have. 

The relationship feels rushed and done through a lot of classic Hollywood shorthand and hand waving. The two fall madly in love in an afternoon and it’s never worked for me.

The first time I saw it, the ending happened suddenly and shocked me, but it also had a great sense of finality and completeness for me. It felt "right" for the movie. It fit the tone of the movie and the music. Just as how the real Judy now looked like the fake Madeleine, Madeleine's death really happened to her. It also fit in that her death was a consequence both of Scottie indulging his obsession by forcing a completely different person (to his knowledge) with her own life and feelings to look like his dead fantasy, and of his spiteful choice to drag her to the scene of the crime just to rub in her face that he now knew the truth. To me, changing her, exposing her so spitefully like that, and still kissing her afterwards were all crazy, so a nun scaring her out a window to her death after all that just felt like par for the course. 

What I found interesting on my second viewing was the relief in tension when Scottie is finally done changing Judy to look like Madeleine. You can see her relax and think that maybe because she is still allowed to be herself in personality that it means he can really love her after all, when the truth is that he doesn't care at all about her personality.

Vertigo has never really been my favorite Hitchcock (probably not even top 3 tbh) and the ending is one the of reasons why. This is just a personal taste thing, but for me it almost feels like finding out the whole movie was a dream. Why go through all the drama and tension just for the very last moment to be so random and out of the blue? 

Although honestly the other responses here are really interesting interpretations so I might be rethinking my opinion 😅

One of the ways to think about her end is to remember Hitchcock's run-ins with the Hays code. The code says crime must be punished. There can be no happy end, because she has helped commit murder. But this is also his punishment. Not only did he convert her to a dead woman (in his mind), forcing her to dress a certain way, change her hair, apply make up just so...this is perverted and the sexual "perversion" is the less than subtle subtext running through their dialogue when she says "you can't even touch me!" And " if I let you change me will it do it? Will you love me?" So I think Hitchcock is suggesting that in Code logic Johnny (the man with many names) is also a criminal and his punishment is to be cured--of his acrophobia--but also 'cured' of the source of his obsessions. Her death is his metaphorical death.

I love this take from Dave Kehr:

> One of the landmarks—not merely of the movies, but of 20th-century art. Alfred Hitchcock’s 1958 film extends the theme of Rear Window—the relationship of creator and creation—into the realm of love and sexuality, focusing on an isolated, inspired romantic (James Stewart) who pursues the spirit of a woman (the powerfully carnal Kim Novak). The film’s dynamics of chase, capture, and escape parallel the artist’s struggle with his work; the enraptured gaze of the Stewart character before the phantom he has created parallels the spectator’s position in front of the movie screen. The famous motif of the fall is presented in horizontal rather than vertical space, so that it becomes not a satanic fall from grace, but a modernist fall into the image, into the artwork—a total absorption of the creator by his creation, which in the end is shown as synonymous with death. But a thematic analysis can only scratch the surface of this extraordinarily dense and commanding film, perhaps the most intensely personal movie to emerge from the Hollywood cinema.

>the ending and the movie itself only work if you buy the central romance

I disagree.  Profoundly.  To what central romance do you refer?

Is Scottie in love?  With whom?  (And who might be in love with him?)

1. Midge?  She sits there in front of Scottie pining away for him for much of the movie; they talk of old times; but he typically ignores her as an object of love.

2. Carlotta?  Elster and the bookseller tell him of Carlotta.  Scottie dreams of Carlotta.  But she can hardly be any thing else than a myth to him than someone to love.

3. The real Madeleine, Elster's wife?  But Scottie never meets her alive in the flesh, never speaks with her.  He sees her corpse on the roof of the church.  (He loves a corpse--surely that is the "central romance," isn't it?)

4. Judy-as-Madeleine 1, whom Elster creates for Scottie?  She isn't real.

5. Judy-as-Madeleine 2, whom Scottie creates for himself?  But she too isn't real.

6. Judy Barton?  But to Scottie she is much like Midge.  She is real to him but he doesn't want her--he wants "Madeleine."  Maybe.

7.  etc.--yes, there are other "things" Scottie seems in love with, but I will not discuss them here.  They are just as obvious as the items above.

So, perhaps you will forgive me if I take your "central romance" with an enormous mountain of salt.  And your "I can appreciate it" doesn't seem accurate--if you appreciated it, I am unsure you would simplify it to some unstated "central romance"--e.g. the typical expected Hollywood one, the one between elegantly clothed, illuminated, and photographed Stewart and Novak in some iteration for your viewing pleasure.

>The relationship feels rushed

Which relationship?  You pretend there is only one.  I am aware of several.  None seems rushed.  Each impinges upon the others.

>classic Hollywood shorthand and hand waving

Yes, that is exactly what this movie is *not*--a classic Hollywood movie with a typical Hollywood central romance and even typical Hollywood hand waving about this or that.  The movie does not offer hand waving but something utterly different.  From your comment you seem unaware of it.

>The two fall madly in love in an afternoon and it’s never worked for me.

Who?  Which two?  (See the list above.  Oh, you are still stuck on Stewart and Novak.  I'm not.  I do not expect or demand the movie to be what I want it to be.  I accept what it offers me.)

I think your comment is evidence you miss much of what the movie offers.

I like this movie more and more every time I see it, and I have seen it many times.

I think the cruelty that you detect is a product of how much the director's obsessions and fetishes are embedded in the film. Watching "Vertigo", you could see a hapless man falling into a trap out of love, but you could also see a controlling man clinging to an idea of female beauty with no regard for reality. In this second reading, you can see some of Hitchcock's mindset. Although it is commendable that he takes Judy's side for a bit, ultimately the movie is about Scottie and his rude awakening (Judy's life being the price to pay for curing Scottie's vertigo is an unsavory idea, but of course the film is problematic in many areas, even though it's considered a masterpiece).

What a weirdly condescending comment. Regardless, the central romance in the movie is Judy-as-Madeline. And Scottie goes from showing up on her doorstep to professing his love for her in a day. 

It always struck me as rushed.

Which "Judy-as-Madeleine"?  Elster's version or Scottie's?

Yes, I do again disagree with you.  Indeed:

> to professing his love for her in a day.

demonstrates to me there is something off about your statement.  You ignore all the other loves in the movie which intertwine with each other.  It is not that he professes his love for her out of the blue--he has already implicitly "professed" love over and over for objects of his obsession.  Those other loves prepare the way.  He is obsessed.  There is nothing rushed with obsession--or there is, and it is such a personal part of his psyche that an outside cannot judge.

I don't see how my previous comment was condescending.  I wished too establish a context with the list.  If my list offended you, I apologize.
I’m good.
How would his vertigo be a manifestation of his death drive? Isn't his vertigo basically a PTSD response to heights caused by almost falling to his death?

Yes, you could say that Scottie wishes to fool himself. He may simply have been trying to make Judy look as much like Madeleine as possible, but if he could reach the point where he truly thought she was the Madeleine he knew and not a different woman named Judy, then I think he'd go for that. 

Anyway, I would also say that the central romance is between Scottie and Judy, even though Scottie is only in love with Judy-as-Madeleine. He falls in love with Judy-as-Madeleine 1, but Judy herself also falls in love with Scottie at this time.

*Rear Window* and *North By Northwest* are definitely up there, and then one that's a little less well known but that I adore is *The Lady Vanishes*! It has mystery, romance, tons of humor, and really fascinating satire of the British psyche in the lead up to WWII. Also from around that period I love *The 39 Steps* and *Foreign Correspondent.*
